description: DeForPact, short for “Design For Impact”, is a team that uses design and storytelling to bring important topics to the world. For Space Apps, we turned NASA’s retired explorers into a storybook for young readers.
summary: “NASA’s Space Time Capsules” is a digital storybook for children that introduces eight NASA missions, from Surveyor 1 on the Moon to the Voyager probes in interstellar space. Each chapter explains why the machine was sent, how it worked, and what it taught us, with a fact, a thinking question, and a read-aloud option.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
“NASA’s Space Time Capsules” is a digital storybook that introduces children to eight NASA missions: Surveyor 1, the Apollo science stations (ALSEP), Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance and Ingenuity, and Voyager 1 and 2. Readers tap a chapter to open it. Each chapter has a picture, a short story, “What did this explorer teach us?”, a “Space-fact!” box, and a “Think like a space scientist” question. Readers can filter chapters by Moon, Mars, and Deep space, or listen to a chapter read aloud. A checkbox on each chapter tracks progress, and exploring all eight earns a “Mission Specialist” badge. At the end are four challenge questions and a mini space dictionary.

What benefits does it have?
Young readers mostly hear about active missions, while the earlier landers, rovers, and probes are usually explained in dense technical pages. Our storybook explains how each machine worked and what it discovered in plain language, with the facts kept accurate. It works on phones, which most students use, and it needs no installation or login. The read-aloud option helps younger readers and those who prefer listening.

What is the intended impact?
We want students to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and see how engineering led to scientific discoveries. The thinking questions encourage curiosity, and teachers or parents can use the book for classroom reading and discussion. Our goal is to inspire the next generation of space scientists and engineers.

What tools, languages, and software did we use?

  • Writing and layout: Microsoft Word for the storybook text and pictures. Deployed on Netlify as a digital storybook in web page format.
  • Web page: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, built as a single self-contained page.
  • Accessibility features: the browser’s built-in read-aloud (speech synthesis), responsive layout, and dark mode.
  • AI assistance: Claude (by Anthropic) helped research the missions, check facts, and build the web page from our text. Our team wrote and reviewed the content.
  • NASA resources: mission facts and dates adapted from NASA and NASA/JPL-Caltech material.

How is it creative?
Instead of a plain list of facts, each machine’s mission is told as a short adventure, with “Space-fact!” and “Think like a space scientist” features that make readers part of the story. The explorer-badge and read-aloud features make learning feel like a game, and the stories follow the full timeline from the 1960s Moon landings to Voyager in interstellar space.

What factors did we consider?

  • Audience: the language and examples are written for school-age children.
  • Accuracy: dates and numbers were checked against NASA sources and corrected where needed.
  • Accessibility: a layout that works on phones, large readable text, read-aloud, and dark mode.
  • Honest status: we described each spacecraft’s current status as of 14 November 2026, noting which are silent and which still operate.
  • Image credits and AI use: we are disclosing the sources of our pictures (from Nasa resources) and our use of AI, as the challenge requires.
